2.1.2 Key Considerations A. Rainfall (A Non-Negotiable Factor) • Rainfall is one of the most critical parameters because it cannot be artificially controlled or adjusted. Locations with rainfall within the recommended range of 2000–3000 mm annually are highly preferred, as they ensure sufficient water for tree hydration, flowering, and fruiting.
B. Soil and Terrain (Factors That Can Be Improved) • Parameters such as soil type, pH, salinity, and drainage can often be corrected through soil treatments or engineered solutions:
• Soil pH: Adjusted with lime (to increase pH) or sulfur (to lower pH).
• Soil Salinity: Reduced through soil washing or the application of gypsum.

• Soil pH: Adjusted with lime (to increase pH) or sulfur (to lower pH).
• Soil Salinity: Reduced through soil washing or the application of gypsum.
• Drainage: Improved with engineered drainage systems or reshaping the terrain.
• Soil Fertility: Enhanced through the addition of organic matter, compost, or fertilizers.
C. Sea Level and Slope (Minimal Concern) • Sea level and slope are less critical factors compared to rainfall and soil parameters. Flat terrains or low-altitude locations can be optimized through proper design and engineering, such as implementing terracing or ensuring adequate water flow.
2.1.3 Case Study Example When comparing two potential locations:
Site A: Receives rainfall within the ideal range but has poor soil quality.
Site B: Has better soil quality but excessive rainfall beyond the recommended range.

In this scenario, Site B would be the preferred choice because soil quality is the most critical factor for long-term productivity. Even though Site B receives excessive rainfall, this issue can be managed by implementing an effective drainage system. In contrast, poor soil quality at Site A would pose a more significant challenge, as degraded soil limits plant growth and may require extensive remediation efforts that are not always successful.
This highlights the importance of prioritizing fundamental factors like soil quality over environmental conditions that can be controlled through infrastructure improvements.

This process involves the complete removal of previous vegetation, including oil palm, rubber trees, old orchards, or secondary forests, using excavators and other heavy machinery. A well-executed land clearing process eliminates potential threats to durian trees and provides an optimal foundation for long-term orchard productivity. It ensures: A clean and disease-free soil environment for young durian trees. Better pest management by removing old tree residues that attract harmful insects. Improved soil aeration and structure, promoting healthy root growth. Efficient drainage, reducing the risk of root rot and other water- related diseases.

A. Complete Removal of Previous Crops If the land was previously cultivated with oil palm or rubber trees, the clearing process must be extremely thorough. All roots, stumps, and residual plant materials must be completely removed to prevent the risk of disease carryover and pest infestation.
• Disease Prevention: Old tree residues may harbor fungal pathogens, bacterial infections, and harmful nematodes that can affect young durian trees.
• Pest Control: Leftover roots and decomposing plant matter can attract ants, termites, and other harmful insects, which may damage durian saplings.

B. Key Performance Parameter of Centrifugal Pump To ensure efficient and reliable operation of centrifugal pumps in our irrigation system, the following key performance parameters must be monitored and maintained.

nsure efficient and reliable operation of centrifugal pumps in our irrigation system, the following key performance parameters must be monitored and maintained.
Capacity: • Capacity means the flow rate with which liquid is moved or pushed by the pump to the desired point in the process. • It is commonly measured in either gallons per minute ( gpm) or cubic meters per hour (m3/hr).
Head: • The term “head” is used instead of “pressure” to describe the pump’s performance. • Head represents the height to which the pump can raise a liquid, based on the energy imparted by the pump to the liquid. • This is measured in feet or meters of liquid column and is not influenced by the liquid’s specific gravity (weight).

• Distance of Throw: This refers to the radius of water distribution from the sprinkler. We choose sprinklers with a throw distance that allows for optimal coverage around each durian tree, ensuring water reaches the root zone effectively.
• Application Rate: Also known as the precipitation rate, this measures how quickly water is applied to the soil. We select sprinklers with an application rate suited to the soil’s absorption capacity, minimizing runoff and ensuring efficient water usage.
• Distribution Uniformity (DU): This factor indicates how evenly water is applied over the area.

• Distribution Uniformity (DU): This factor indicates how evenly water is applied over the area. High distribution uniformity is essential to prevent overwatering in certain zones and underwatering in others, promoting consistent soil moisture levels across the orchard.
D. Sprinkler Placement To ensure even water distribution and efficient coverage, the placement of sprinklers around durian trees follows specific guidelines.
• Distance from Trees: Each sprinkler should be placed at a distance that maximizes root zone coverage without causing direct spray on the tree trunk. This distance may vary depending on tree age and growth stage.
• Spacing Between Sprinklers: Sprinklers are spaced to create overlapping coverage zones, reducing dry areas and promoting consistent soil moisture levels across the orchard.
